rules.description: A controls fault that halts a production line is functionally the same as a mechanical failure from the plant's point of view: the line is not running. The fix, though, usually starts with an engineer looking at the program remotely rather than a truck being dispatched, because most PLC and HMI faults are resolvable over a remote connection faster than any technician can drive to site. The first rung reflects that, but its wait is kept short enough that a real down line does not stall waiting on a login. The second rung names the assigned controls engineer for this program specifically, not a general on call technician, because a fault in this rung of ladder logic usually needs someone who has already worked in this program's I/O map and naming convention, and a generalist who has never opened it can lose the first hour just getting oriented. Relationship is ignored because a stopped line is not less urgent for a first time customer.

fallback.notes: A live human confirms an engineer is engaged. A PLC fault left on voicemail is a line that stays down until someone happens to check messages.

rules.description: A fault that surfaces during a commissioning window, before the line has ever run production, often has no documented asset_criticality yet because the criticality assessment has not been finalized against a live production schedule, and the relationship is usually new since commissioning is most often a first job for that line. Elsewhere in this matrix an unresolved criticality defaults to priority 2 through default_rule, deliberately, because most unknowns are genuinely ambiguous and worth a human sorting them out. Commissioning is the deliberate exception. A fault that blocks a scheduled go live is time boxed against a customer's production start date, with people who already traveled to be there for it, so this rule treats a new relationship plus an unresolved criticality plus an active fault as priority 1 rather than waiting for someone to first resolve the ambiguity.

fallback.notes: A commissioning window has a scheduled end date attached to it. An automated ending here just delays the discovery that the schedule has already slipped.

rules.description: A degraded or intermittent controls fault on a line with a documented criticality and an established relationship still gets a real ladder and a stated response window, even though it is not treated as a full stop. Remote diagnosis is still attempted first for the same reason it is attempted on a full stop: most of these faults do not need a truck roll to resolve.

fallback.notes: A committed callback window is stated to the caller and recorded, not a promise to call back at some point.

rules.description: A first time caller during business hours with no active fault, typically a request for a quote on a new machine build, a retrofit, or a new integration project. This is the path most often lost to slow response rather than to price, so it gets a real ladder rather than a voicemail box.

fallback.notes: A committed callback means a specific window is stated to the caller and recorded, not a promise to call back at some point.

rules.description: Scheduled program backups, documentation updates, and minor HMI cosmetic requests on ancillary equipment with no production tie in.

default_rule.description: Anything the classifier could not place on the criticality or condition axes. Treated as priority 2, not priority 4, because an unclassified controls call could be a documentation question or it could be a line that just faulted with a caller who does not yet know how to describe the fault code they are looking at. The cheapest way to tell the difference is to have a human ask.

fallback.notes: Unclassified plus voicemail is how a real line down event becomes a Monday morning discovery.
